name: Bonesmashing
lead: Bonesmashing (also written bone smashing, and sometimes called face hammering) is a looksmaxxing practice in which people strike their own facial bones, typically with a hammer or another blunt object, in the belief that the impact will make the bone remodel into a more defined, "chiselled" shape [1][8]. The features most often named are the cheekbones (zygomas), jawline and brow ridge, which practitioners associate with a more angular, masculine-looking face. It sits in the "hardmaxxing" or bonehacks end of looksmaxxing, alongside surgery and drug use, as opposed to "softmaxxing" practices such as skincare or grooming [1].

The idea is usually justified by reference to Wolff's law, the nineteenth-century principle that bone adapts to the mechanical loads placed on it, and to the belief that healed bone comes back stronger or larger [9][10]. Looksmaxxing forum members have posted before-and-after photographs and thread titles crediting bonesmashing for changes to the brow, eye area or cheekbones, while other members reply that the changes reflect puberty, camera angles or editing [5][6][11][12].

Wikipedia describes the practice as an inside joke that is rarely carried out [1]. It has nonetheless attracted a large amount of attention. Surgeons published letters in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery in 2024 describing it as a dangerous TikTok trend [2][3], a nursing journal published a risk article [7], a 2026 study of social-media discourse counted thousands of mentions of the term [4], and news outlets from 2023 onwards have run stories quoting plastic, reconstructive and maxillofacial surgeons on it [13][14][15][16]. No clinical study has tested whether striking the facial skeleton changes its shape.

chain: Repeated blunt impact to cheekbone, jaw or brow
Believers expect bone to remodel and thicken as it heals
A sharper, more defined facial contour (claimed)
angle.text: Practitioners aim for a more angular face by striking the zygomas, jaw or brow, reasoning from Wolff's law that bone responds to stress by building more bone. This outcome is claimed by proponents; surgeons quoted in the press say it is not an established way to change facial structure and describe injury risks [13][14][15].

paras: Bonesmashing refers to deliberately striking a part of the facial skeleton, using a hammer, a rolling pin, a fist or a similar object, with the stated goal of changing its shape [1][8]. Descriptions in the press and in surgical commentary single out the cheekbones, jaw angle, chin and brow ridge as the usual targets, because those are the features forums associate with an attractive male face [13][15][17].

The practice is classed by looksmaxxing writers as hardmaxxing: a more extreme tier of appearance modification than softmaxxing, a group that covers skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness. Hardmaxxing also includes off-label drug use and cosmetic surgery [1]. Within that group, bonesmashing is typically described as the do-it-yourself, non-surgical counterpart to procedures such as osteotomy or implants, which are performed by surgeons under anaesthesia [8].

Looksmaxxing developed in the 2010s on forums sometimes grouped as the PSL community, and moved to wider audiences, notably through TikTok, in the early 2020s [1]. Wikipedia does not say where bonesmashing specifically began [1]. Grokipedia's AI-generated entry places the emergence of the term in online communities around 2020 and says it began partly as a satirical or exaggerated idea before some participants adopted it seriously; its own start dates are inconsistent, and the account is therefore given with caution [8].

By late 2023 coverage was describing a TikTok trend. CBS Baltimore reported that videos on the subject had passed 250 million views [13], and a Grokipedia summary of other coverage reports a figure of about 260 million for the #bonesmashing hashtag in October 2023 [8]. Wikipedia cites news pieces from Vice (June 2023), The Daily Dot and CBS Baltimore (November 2023), Esquire (December 2023) and The Guardian (February 2024) as part of the coverage [1].

In February 2026 the Kick streamer and looksmaxxing figure known as Clavicular said on a stream that he had hit his own face with a hammer to enlarge his jawline, an account that UNILAD Tech reported along with a dermatologist's rebuttal and with commenters who credited his appearance to other procedures [16]. A Vice piece published on 1 March 2026 returned to the subject with comment from an oral and maxillofacial surgeon [14]. In April 2026 a Brisbane hospital published a warning from one of its plastic surgeons about the trend [15].

Proponents most often cite Wolff's law. Named for the German anatomist and surgeon Julius Wolff (1836 to 1902), who published his account in 1892, it holds that healthy bone adapts to the loads placed on it, with changes first in the internal trabecular structure and later in the outer cortex [9]. The remodelling is understood to run through mechanotransduction, in which bone cells called osteocytes sense strain and fluid flow and signal other cells, and the effect depends on the duration, magnitude and rate of loading. Wikipedia notes that the law is considered a simplification refined by later work, such as Harold Frost's mechanostat theory [9].

Bonesmashers extend this to say that impact trauma, or the microfractures it produces, will cause the face to lay down extra bone or to heal thicker and stronger [10][16]. Clavicular described the aim as microfractures that heal stronger [16]. Surgeons responding in the press say that Wolff's law describes adaptation to loading over time, not a response to fracture, and that repair tissue generally does not return stronger than the original. Plastic surgeon Ben Schultz said healed tissue typically regains around 80 percent of its original strength [10]. Mater's Dr Diana Kennedy said the videos misinterpret the principle [15]. The Wikipedia article on Wolff's law itself cites a New York Times piece saying there is no evidence that a broken bone heals stronger than before [9].

Participants in looksmaxxing forums discuss bonesmashing both as a technique and as a point of dispute. Some posters share timelines and photos, such as a thread of progress pictures from age 14 to 15 whose author himself allowed that puberty might be responsible [5]. Other thread titles claim changes to the glabella (the area between the brows) and the eye area attributed to the practice [11][12]. A separate thread asks outright whether it is real or "cope", with replies ranging from "works" to accusations of exaggeration [6].

Skeptical posters on the same forums point to puberty, lens distortion and image editing as the real causes, with one reply to a results thread saying the photos "looks morphed" [5][6]. A Hacker News submission in 2026 titled "Bonesmashing: Inside The Extreme Looksmaxxer Technique" shows the practice also being discussed outside looksmaxxing-specific spaces [18].

Because the wiki documents the practice rather than instructing it, only general features are given. Accounts in the press and in Clavicular's own description say that practitioners act on their own, without medical supervision, using ordinary objects and targeting one facial site at a time [16][17]. Proponents describe doing so repeatedly over weeks or months and judging progress with photographs, which is why timeline posts are a common format on forums [5].

Surgeons and journalists contrast this with how fractures are handled clinically. In facial surgery, bone is cut or repositioned with planning, imaging and fixation, and clinicians quoted in coverage direct people who want a change in facial structure to a board-certified surgeon rather than home methods [14][15].

No published study has measured the effect of bonesmashing in people. The published literature consists of commentary and social-media analysis. In 2024 letters in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, one of them titled as an urgent concern about a dangerous TikTok trend and another about the excesses of social-networking trends, called attention to the practice [2][3]. A 2024 article in Nursing discussed the risks of the trend [7].

A 2026 cross-sectional study in the same journal analysed online discourse about do-it-yourself facial aesthetic trends, using social-listening tools, Google Trends and Instagram engagement metrics, followed by a thematic analysis of the 100 most engaged looksmaxxing posts. For bonesmashing it recorded 2,518 mentions over twelve months, an estimated social-media reach of 32 million and about 2.5 million interactions over three months, with YouTube carrying the largest share of discussion [4].

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article summarises criticism by facial surgeons that bonesmashing carries a risk of fractures, facial misalignment, neurovascular injury, deformity and changes in vision [1]. Dermatologist Andrea Suarez, responding to Clavicular, said blunt trauma does not build stronger bone and warned of disfigurement and scarring surgery [16]. Vice quotes New Jersey oral and maxillofacial surgeon Lee Kojanis as saying it does not reliably improve appearance [14].

Clinicians quoted in coverage describe the face as densely supplied with blood vessels and nerves. Ben Schultz said bleeding could obstruct the airway or threaten vision and that nerve injury was possible, and he described osteophytes, bony outgrowths, as a possible outcome [10]. Lee Kojanis listed fractures of the jaw, cheekbone or orbit, effects on vision, bite and jaw-joint problems, dental and gum injury, nerve injury, infection and asymmetric healing [14].

Dr Diana Kennedy of Mater Private Hospital Brisbane listed soft-tissue swelling and microfractures, scarring with possible nerve damage, permanent disfigurement that may become more visible with age, damage to bite and chewing, and the possible need for emergency surgery to drain blood collections or repair fractures [15]. Grokipedia additionally lists tooth loss, concussion and woven-bone healing that may not restore original strength; these points come from an AI-generated page and are attributed to its summary of other coverage [8].

Coverage began as explainers on a viral trend and shifted to profiles of looksmaxxing influencers. Wikipedia lists Vice (Ruchira Sharma, 7 June 2023), The Daily Dot (8 November 2023), CBS Baltimore (6 November 2023), Esquire (22 December 2023) and The Guardian (15 February 2024) [1]. CBS Baltimore described it as a dangerous TikTok beauty trend that surgeons warn against and quoted Dr Ben Schultz of LifeBridge Health [10][13]. Vice returned in 2026 with a feature quoting Lee Kojanis [14].
In 2026 attention centred on Clavicular, a prominent streamer within looksmaxxing, whose comments about hammering his zygomas prompted both news items and a dermatologist's video response [16][1].

Within looksmaxxing, bonesmashing is a recurring subject on forums, where it is treated variously as a genuine technique, a joke and a point of contention. Wikipedia characterises it as an inside joke that is rarely done [1], while Grokipedia describes it as having moved from satire to something some participants take seriously [8]. Replies to results threads tend to ask whether apparent changes could be puberty or editing [5][6]. The 2026 discourse study lists bonesmashing alongside mewing and do-it-yourself chemical peels and self-injection as social-media trends of interest to facial surgeons [4].
No studies found. Related literature is limited to surgeon commentary letters and a social-media discourse analysis, which describe the trend and do not measure effects on facial structure [2][3][4].

timeline.event: Julius Wolff publishes his account of bone remodelling in response to load, later called Wolff's law and cited by bonesmashing proponents [9].
Looksmaxxing develops on the PSL forums and related incel and manosphere communities [1].
The term bonesmashing appears in online looksmaxxing communities, according to an AI-generated summary with inconsistent dating [8].
Coverage by Vice (June), CBS Baltimore and The Daily Dot (November) and Esquire (December); TikTok videos reported above 250 million views [1][13].
The Guardian (February) and surgical-journal letters, plus a Nursing article, address the trend [1][2][3][7].
Streamer Clavicular describes hammering his zygomas; dermatologist Andrea Suarez responds [16].
Vice publishes a feature with comment from oral and maxillofacial surgeon Lee Kojanis [14].
Mater Private Hospital Brisbane issues a surgeon's warning about the trend [15].
A cross-sectional study of looksmaxxing social-media discourse is published, recording 2,518 mentions of bonesmashing in twelve months [4].

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums bonesmashing is debated as a technique, with some members posting claimed results and others attributing changes to puberty, camera angle or editing [5][6][11].

claims.claim: Hitting facial bones makes them grow or reshape ("it works").
claims.believers: Some forum members post progress photos and thread titles saying bonesmashing changed their glabella, eye area, cheek or brow [5][11][12].
claims.experts: No published study has examined whether striking facial bone changes its shape; surgeons quoted in the press describe fracture, nerve and vision risks [1][13][14].

claims.claim: Wolff's law shows that bone rebuilds stronger and bigger after impact.
claims.believers: Proponents say bone adapts to stress, so repeated impact should thicken it; Clavicular described microfractures healing stronger [16].
claims.experts: Surgeons say Wolff's law describes adaptation to loading, not repair after fracture, and that healed tissue typically regains about 80 percent of its original strength [10][15]; the Wikipedia article on the law cites a report that fractured bone does not heal stronger [9].

claims.claim: Visible changes in before-and-after photos are caused by bonesmashing rather than puberty or other factors.
claims.believers: Posters sharing results credit the practice for changes over months [5].
claims.experts: Other forum members respond that apparent changes are puberty or image manipulation [5][6]; no controlled data exist.

claims.claim: The practice is mostly a joke and few people actually do it.
claims.believers: Wikipedia describes it as an inside joke that is rarely done [1], and forum posters ask whether it is "cope" [6].
claims.experts: A 2026 study logged 2,518 online mentions over twelve months, and surgeons say they have seen real interest, though mentions do not measure how many people act on it [4][14].

claims.claim: Smashing is a do-it-yourself version of facial surgery such as osteotomy.
claims.believers: Proponents present it as a free alternative to surgical changes in jaw or cheek structure [8].
claims.experts: Surgeons say surgical bone procedures are planned, imaged and fixated by specialists, and that unsupervised trauma risks asymmetric healing and nerve injury [14][15].

claims.believers: Followers point to streamers who say they used the method, such as Clavicular [16].
claims.experts: A dermatologist said blunt trauma will not build stronger bone, and commenters noted the streamer's appearance may reflect other procedures [16].

card.summary: Hitting your own facial bones to reshape them; no study supports it and surgeons warn of fractures and nerve damage.
card.note: Surgeons warn of fracture, nerve and vision injury.

quick.overview:
Bonesmashing means striking facial bones, often with a hammer, in the hope of remodeling them into a sharper shape. It is a bonehacks practice in looksmaxxing, and Wikipedia says it is rarely actually done.

No clinical study has tested it. Surgeons have published letters warning about it as a social-media trend.
quick.mechanism: Believers say repeated impact stimulates bone to remodel. This mechanism has not been studied in the context of facial aesthetics.
quick.risks: Surgeons cite fractures, misalignment, neurovascular injury, deformity and vision changes as possible outcomes.
